Q: Deserializing ScalaPB enum from int value and class A:

Yes, you can get the ScalaPB enum companion from the Class[_], but not via getMethod("companion"). Scala companion objects are compiled as a separate “module” class named <EnumClassName>$ with a static field MODULE$ holding the singleton instance. Once you have that instance, call fromValue(int) on it (that’s exactly what GeneratedEnumCompanion is for).

Typical pattern (Scala 2 / ScalaPB):

override def read(kryo: Kryo, input: Input, enumClass: Class[scalapb.GeneratedEnum])
  : scalapb.GeneratedEnum = {

  val v = input.readInt(true)

  val moduleCls = Class.forName(enumClass.getName + "$", true, enumClass.getClassLoader)
  val companion = moduleCls.getField("MODULE$").get(null)
    .asInstanceOf[scalapb.GeneratedEnumCompanion[scalapb.GeneratedEnum]]

  companion.fromValue(v)
}

This assumes enumClass refers to the enum value class, not the companion/module class.

Q: constexpr function call count A:

In GCC & MSVC, there's a macro called _COUNTER_. Use that.

Q: Why use bzero over memset? A:

The one advantage that I think bzero() has over memset() for setting memory to zero is that there's a reduced chance of a mistake being made.

More than once I've come across a bug that looked like:

memset(someobject, size_of_object, 0);    // clear object

The compiler won't complain (though maybe cranking up some warning levels might on some compilers) and the effect will be that the memory isn't cleared. Because this doesn't trash the object - it just leaves it alone - there's a decent chance that the bug might not manifest into anything obvious.

The fact that bzero() isn't standard is a minor irritant. (FWIW, I wouldn't be surprised if most function calls in my programs are non-standard; in fact writing such functions is kind of my job).

In a comment to another answer here, Aaron Newton cited the following from Unix Network Programming, Volume 1, 3rd Edition by Stevens, et al., Section 1.2 (emphasis added):

bzero is not an ANSI C function. It is derived from early Berkely networking code. Nevertheless, we use it throughout the text, instead of the ANSI C memset function, because bzero is easier to remember (with only two arguments) than memset (with three arguments). Almost every vendor that supports the sockets API also provides bzero, and if not, we provide a macro definition in our unp.h header.

Indeed, the author of TCPv3 [TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 3 - Stevens 1996] made the mistake of swapping the second and third arguments to memset in 10 occurrences in the first printing. A C compiler cannot catch this error because both arguments are of the same type. (Actually, the second argument is an int and the third argument is size_t, which is typically an unsigned int, but the values specified, 0 and 16, respectively, are still acceptable for the other type of argument.) The call to memset still worked, because only a few of the socket functions actually require that the final 8 bytes of an Internet socket address structure be set to 0. Nevertheless, it was an error, and one that could be avoided by using bzero, because swapping the two arguments to bzero will always be caught by the C compiler if function prototypes are used.

I also believe that the vast majority of calls to memset() are to zero memory, so why not use an API that is tailored to that use case?

A possible drawback to bzero() is that compilers might be more likely to optimize memcpy() because it's standard and so they might be written to recognize it. However, keep in mind that correct code is still better than incorrect code that's been optimized. In most cases, using bzero() will not cause a noticeable impact on your program's performance, and that bzero() can be a macro or inline function that expands to memset().

Q: Chrome 122 - How to allow insecure content? (Insecure download blocked) A:

If one cannot change any Chrome options (e.g., on ChromeOS) or flags, all is not lost.

Looking in one's Downloads folder (using the shell, not CTRL+J) one can still find the temporary version of the (already!) downloaded file, which one can then simply rename to the permanent version, by hand.

Q: Error with primary key when inserting into Access with node-adodb A:

This is the correct way of creating the Access table.
You need to change ID to an AutoNumber (Counter) field

CREATE TABLE [Sets] 
(
    ID COUNTER CONSTRAINT PK_Sets PRIMARY KEY,
    # rest
);

If you use this, then your insert without ID will work.

Q: How to safely pass training argument to Keras layers in a dynamic list when I don’t know if each layer supports it? A:

In Keras, training is a “privileged” kwarg: when you call a layer as layer(x, training=...), Keras Layer.__call__() inspects the layer’s call() signature and only forwards training if that call() actually declares it (otherwise it’s silently dropped). That’s what people mean by “signature-based filtering.”

So you don’t need try/except at all, just always pass training:

class SingleConv(tf.keras.layers.Layer):
    def __init__(self, ...):
        super().__init__()
        self.module_layers = [ ... ]  # your sublayers

    def call(self, inputs, training=None):
        x = inputs
        for layer in self.module_layers:
            x = layer(x, training=training)  # safe: ignored by layers that don't accept it
        return x

This is the clean/best-practice approach because it avoids exception handling in the hot path (and avoids weirdness under tf.function). If you mix in non-Keras callables (plain functions), then you’d need to handle those separately.

Here is the official documentation example: TensorFlow

Q: How to set timeout for function execution in postgresql? A:

You can’t make PL/pgSQL “self‑terminate” after 2 minutes from inside the function.
The timeout has to be enforced by the session around the call, using statement_timeout (and optionally lock_timeout / transaction_timeout).

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION do_partition_work(p_day date)
RETURNS void
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS
$$
BEGIN
    -- Simulate heavy work for one day’s partition
    PERFORM pg_sleep(30);  -- here you would do CREATE TABLE / ATTACH PARTITION ...
END;
$$;


CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION partition_creator(p_start date, p_count_days integer)
RETURNS void
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS
$$
DECLARE
    d date;
BEGIN
    FOR d IN
        SELECT p_start + i
        FROM generate_series(0, p_count_days - 1) AS g(i)
    LOOP
        PERFORM do_partition_work(d);  -- real logic per day
    END LOOP;
END;
$$;
